# Intro

## Cherish Your Data

\

Without data, there is no data science

. . .

\

I like to differentiate our roles into 2 categories

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment}
[Consuming data]{.mdlit}

You as the consumer of data created by others
:::

::: {.column .fragment}
[Creating Data]{.hilit}

You as the creator/curator of data 
:::
::::


## What to share

- Raw data
- Metadata
- Scripts/code to process data
- License for data


## Raw Data

- Raw data: unprocessed form of the data
- Raw data is sacred: don't touch it! (leave it as is)
- Separate raw data from processed/cleaned data
- Separate data from code


# Metadata

## About Metadata

- Data about the data
- AKA: Codebook
- AKA: Data Dictionary (not to be confused with a python dictionary)
. . .

::: {.poll .fragment}
It is a comprehensive reference document that defines, structures, and explains 
the contents, layout, and variables of a dataset.
:::


## Metadata

- Preferably in a text file
- Include details
    + source, organization
    + background
    + citation*
- Names of variables (features, atttributes)
    + As they appear in the file (usually abbreviations)
    + But also, their full name
- Sometimes you may need to include a full description of each variable

## Metadata (cont'd)

- Recommended data types for each variable
    + boolean, integer, float, character, other
- For categorical or ordinal variables, describe their categories
- Missing values: how are they encoded
- Provenance
    + How was data collected?
    + Who collected it, how was it collected it?
- If necessary, include further details, comments, notes, for how to 
make sense of data, or how to treat certain values.

# Tabular Data

## Data Tables

Tidy Data by Hadley Wickham

<https://vita.had.co.nz/papers/tidy-data.pdf>


Three Core Rules

1. [Each variable is a column]{.bold-hilit} (a column contains all values that measure the same attribute).
2. [Each observation is a row]{.bold-hilit} (a row contains all values measured on a single unit).
3. [Each value is a cell]{.bold-hilit} (a cell contains a single measurement of an attribute).


# FAIR Principles

## FAIR

Data should be

- Findable
- Accessible
- Interoperable
- Reusable


## FAIR

- [Findable:]{.bold-hilit} Does it have an immutable digital tracking link (DOI)?

- [Accessible:]{.bold-hilit} Can you download the data in 2 clicks without an institutional 
login?

- [Interoperable:]{.bold-hilit} Is the data stored in an open-source text format (like .csv), 
or is it trapped in a proprietary Excel format (.xlsx)?

- [Reusable:]{.bold-hilit} Is there an explicit Creative Commons (CC-BY) license attached, 
or is it unlicensed and legally untouchable?

- Important: Just uploading files to the internet doesn't make your science open or useful.


## Share Your Data Online

- Ideally: Deposit your data online in a well-established repository, 
with a permanent identifier

- Deposit data in whatever data archive is the "go to" place for your field.

- Better than nothing: Store it in a google drive, dropbox, box, AWS,
and share a public link to it.


## General Data Repositories

- Dataverse (<http://thedata.org>): A repository for research data that takes 
care of long-term preservation and good archival practices, while researchers 
can share, keep control of, and get recognition for their data.

- FigShare (<http://figshare.com>): A repository where users can make all of their 
research outputs available in a citable, shareable, and discoverable manner.

- Zenodo (<http://zenodo.org>): A repository service that enables users to share 
research results (data and publications) that are not part of existing 
institutional or subject-based repositories.

- Dryad (<http://datadryad.org>): A repository that aims to make data archiving 
as simple as possible through a suite of services not necessarily provided by 
publishers or institutional websites.


## What about sharing data in GitHub?

- Don't use github for big data
- GitHub has a limit on file size: cannot exceed 100MB
- Many data sets can easily exceed 100MB
- Also, be careful with binary data 
(Git tracks text files, not binary files)


## What about sharing data through an R package?

- Interesting option for relatively small data sets.
- Especially good for teaching/learning purposes.
- Example: `"stat20data"` package
- Example: `"janeaustinr"` package
- Example: `"harrypotter"` package


## ROpenSci

- The project R Open Science
- Has tools and packages for accessing lots of data


# Licenses

## Licenses for Data

Including an explicit license with your data is the best way to let others
know exactly what they can and cannot do with the data you shared.

Prefer well established licenses (or waivers) to clearly communicate 
the rights and responsibilities of both the people providing the data
and the people using it.


## Creative Commons Licenses

- [CC BY:]{.bold-hilit} Credit must be given to you, the creator.
<br>
<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>

\

- [CC BY-SA:]{.bold-hilit} Credit must be given to you, the creator.
Adaptations must be shared under the same terms.
<br>
<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/>

\

- [CC BY-ND:]{.bold-hilit} Credit must be given to you, the creator.
No derivatives or adaptations of your work are permitted.
<br>
<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/>


## 

- [CC BY-NC:]{.bold-hilit} Credit must be given to you, the creator.
Only noncommercial use of your work is permitted.
<br>
<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/>

\

- [CC BY-NC-SA:]{.bold-hilit} Credit must be given to you, the creator.
Only noncommercial use of your work is permitted.
Adaptations must be shared under the same terms.
<br>
<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/>

\

- [CC BY-NC-ND:]{.bold-hilit} Credit must be given to you, the creator.

## Open Data Commons licenses

- [Open Data Commons Open Database License (ODbL)]{.bold-hilit}
<br>
"Attribution Share-Alike for data/databases"
<br>
<https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/>

- [Open Data Commons Attribution License]{.bold-hilit}
<br>
"Attribution for data/databases"
<br>
<https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/by/>

- [Open Data Commons Public Domain Dedication and License (PDDL)]{.bold-hilit}
<br>
"Public Domain for data/databases"
<br>
<https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/pddl/>

- To create

As long as you:

- Attribute

- To create

As long as you:

:::
:::

## Last Words

- Love your data, and help others love it, too
- Publish your data
- Encourage others to cherish, document, and publish their data
- Reward colleagues who share data
- Praise those following best practices
- Give credit to those whose data you use
